summary: Specifies an experimental variant of Internet mail that permits non-ASCII characters in email header fields, including in addresses and the information based on them. It is part of a set of experimental documents for fully internationalized email and updates the message format specifications. It was replaced by RFC 6532.

eli5.summary: For a long time email addresses only allowed basic English letters. This experimental plan lets the top part of a message use any language's letters. It has been replaced by RFC 6532.

questions: can email addresses have non-ascii characters
how does utf-8 work in email
subtitle: UTF-8 characters in email headers instead of ASCII encoding

tldr.problem: Email headers traditionally only allow ASCII characters, which prevents users with non-ASCII names from using them in email addresses, display names, and message subjects.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5335 permits Unicode text encoded as UTF-8 to be used directly in email header field bodies, rather than forcing non-ASCII text to be encoded in ASCII-compatible form.
tldr.outcome: This experimental approach was replaced by RFC 6532 with a more mature standard, but it was the first specification to allow native UTF-8 in email headers.

today: RFC 5335 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 6532, which provides a Standards-Track specification for internationalized email headers. Modern email systems should use RFC 6532 instead of this experimental version.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5335 addresses a fundamental limitation of email: the restriction to ASCII characters. Traditionally, email addresses, sender and recipient names, and message subjects could only contain the 26 English letters, digits, and a few punctuation marks. This prevented users with non-ASCII names (such as those in Asian, Arabic, Cyrillic or accented Latin scripts) from using their actual names in email.

The RFC specifies how to extend email to permit UTF-8 encoded text directly in message header field bodies. Rather than encoding non-ASCII text in ASCII-compatible form using MIME encoding (as was previously required), UTF-8 text can now appear as-is in headers, provided the system is authorized by SMTP extension RFC 5336.
sections.eli5: Email used to only work with English letters. This note says you can put any language's letters in the message headers. But both the sender and receiver need to support this new way.

sections.title: The Problem with ASCII-Only Email
sections.content:
Many users worldwide have names not normally expressed with just ASCII characters. RFC 5335 identifies three capabilities needed for full email internationalization:

  • The ability to send non-ASCII content in message bodies (already provided by MIME)
  • The ability to use international characters in envelope addresses (covered by RFC 5336)
  • The ability to express those addresses and related information in mail header fields, including display names, comments, and free text like the Subject field

The traditional format defined by RFC 2822 allows only ASCII in headers. This forces non-ASCII text to be encoded as ASCII-safe sequences using RFC 2047 encoding, which is verbose and not user-friendly. RFC 5335 removes this restriction by permitting UTF-8 text directly.
sections.eli5: When email was invented, it only handled English. To send a message with other alphabets, you had to encode them in a complex format. This note just lets you use the actual letters directly.

sections.title: UTF-8 Syntax and Header Field Rules
sections.content:
RFC 5335 extends the syntax rules from RFC 2822 to allow UTF-8 characters in header field bodies. Header field names remain ASCII-only (such as Subject:, From:, To:), but the values following them can now contain UTF-8.

The RFC defines UTF-8 characters using ABNF rules from RFC 3629, specifying valid byte sequences for the various Unicode ranges (2-byte, 3-byte, and 4-byte sequences). It also applies normalization (NFC form is recommended) to ensure consistent representation of characters with multiple encodings.

Specifically, rules are extended to allow UTF-8 in:

  • Comments (text in parentheses)
  • Quoted strings (text in quotation marks)
  • Unstructured header fields (like Subject)
  • Email addresses (the local part and domain)
sections.eli5: The header field names stay in English, but the content can now have other letters. These must follow the UTF-8 rules so computers understand them correctly.

sections.title: Internationalized Email Addresses
sections.content:
A key change is support for utf8-addr-spec: email addresses where both the local part (before the @) and the domain can contain UTF-8 characters. An address like user@example.com can become 用户@example.com (with a Chinese character in the local part).

RFC 5335 also introduces alt-address: an optional ASCII-only alternative address that can be included for backward compatibility. If a sender sends to 用户@example.com with an alternative of user.alt@example.com, older mail systems can still deliver to the alternative. The procedure for converting between internationalized and ASCII addresses is described in RFC 5504 (downgrading).

The message/global MIME media type is defined for messages that contain UTF-8 headers, allowing them to be transmitted safely when embedded in other messages or over 7-bit-only transports.
sections.eli5: Email addresses can now have any language's letters. If sending to someone on an old mail system, you can provide an English version of the address as a backup.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Allowing longer addresses and variable-width UTF-8 encoding introduces security considerations. The RFC notes that UTF-8 often requires multiple octets per character, making internationalized local parts potentially longer than before. Systems processing email must take care not to overflow buffers or truncate addresses.

A key concern is that when a user has both a non-ASCII address and an ASCII alternative, these might route to different destinations depending on what the intermediate mail server supports. While this could surprise users, it is not considered a protocol flaw.

The security impact on digital signature systems (DKIM, S/MIME, OpenPGP) is discussed, since changing header encodings affects how signatures verify. RFC 4952 provides additional detail on these implications.
sections.eli5: Computers need to be careful to handle the longer addresses without running out of space. And if you have two versions of your address, they might go to different places depending on which mail servers they travel through.

sections.title: Experimental Status
sections.content:
RFC 5335 was published as Experimental, meaning it was a proposal for testing and feedback rather than a complete standard. The mechanism proved successful but was refined in later work.

This RFC updates RFC 2045 (MIME) and RFC 2822 (message format) to allow content-transfer-encoding on the message/global subtype, which was previously prohibited for message subtypes. RFC 5336 and RFC 5337 define the SMTP transport extensions needed to safely transmit these messages.

RFC 5335 was obsoleted by RFC 6532, which provides a mature Standard-Track specification for the same functionality. RFC 6532 incorporates lessons learned from the experimental phase and is the current definition of internationalized email headers.
sections.eli5: This was an experiment to test the idea. It worked well enough that later RFCs made it an official standard (RFC 6532). So if you are using modern email, you should use RFC 6532, not this one.
